newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: Nicaragua's Aleman, Ortega on collision course.
newsitem.headline: Nicaragua's Aleman, Ortega on collision course.

text.p: Four months into his term, Nicaraguan President Arnoldo Aleman appears to be on a collision course with his powerful left-wing rival, former Sandinista President Daniel Ortega.
Their latest clash is over tax reform proposals made by Aleman, a conservative coffee grower. The tax code changes were to be debated in parliament on Wednesday.
The dispute has thrown Nicaragua back into the bitter rancour of the 1996 election campaign between the two men.

The confrontation is not expected to erupt in the violence so often seen in this Central American country's tumultuous history, but street protests crippled the capital and battered a fragile economy since Aleman won power last year.
Ortega, a leftist revolutionary who governed Nicaragua in the 1980s wearing Fidel Castro-style fatigues, wants a larger voice for his Sandinista Front in formulating economic policy.
Aleman, who defeated Ortega in the October election by winning 51 percent of the votes to his 38 percent, said there would be no deals with the Sandinistas.
In an interview with Reuters, Ortega accused Aleman of "prolonging and deepening instability" in Nicaragua.
"The problem is the Liberal Party wants to rule alone ... and that doesn't correspond to the reality of the county," Ortega said.
Postponing a national accord, in which the Sandinistas play a major role, will lead to new protests, he warned.

A five-day national strike led by the Sandinistas in April disrupted public transport, closed universities and dealt a blow to an economy that was rapidly turning around under the Aleman administration.

The strike prompted Aleman to set up "working roundtables" between his government and the Sandinistas, a move that created discord within the ruling Liberal Alliance, leading the most right-wing party to quit the coalition.
"I have not negotiated with the Sandinistas," Aleman told Reuters. "I have opened a channel of communication. At no time have I made a deal or negotiated with the Sandinistas."
The president insisted that the threat of more unrest orchestrated by the Sandinistas had not changed his policies.
"No, no, no, no. I'm continuing the same way," Aleman said. "I want to establish the rule of law in Nicaragua and not the will of one person or of one party."
